strengths: The paper targets an important and insufficiently measured failure mode in generated videos: temporal 3D geometric inconsistency that appearance-oriented metrics can miss. Treating this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution is more appropriate than the default Algorithms/General category; under that framing, the physically motivated local-pose agreement idea is intuitive and potentially useful as a diagnostic.

The pipeline combines static-region isolation, depth-based partitioning, local PnP pose estimation, global-pose comparison, and depth consistency into interpretable components. The supplementary material provides algorithms, hyperparameters, PCA weights, dataset composition, and baseline details that improve reproducibility.

The empirical study is broad, covering 1,296 videos, ten generators from multiple generation paradigms, three real-video domains, several baselines, component ablations, synthetic perturbations, camera-motion analysis, mask-corruption tests, and qualitative examples. The authors also openly expose substantial sensitivity to motion-segmentation errors.
weaknesses: The central benchmark claim lacks convincing construct validation. There are no human judgments of geometric consistency, no correlation with expert annotations, and no evaluation on sequences with known 3D geometry or camera motion. Real videos are merely assumed to be ground-truth-consistent, while lower scores for real data and visually selected examples do not establish that SGC measures the intended property. Likewise, ablation variants are judged largely by whether they produce the desired real-versus-generated separation, making the argument partly circular.

The translation terms appear technically ill-defined across the two independent geometry estimators. Local PnP translations are obtained by back-projecting Video Depth Anything depths, whereas the global translation comes from VGGT; no scale alignment or normalization between their coordinate systems is specified before taking Euclidean differences in Eq. 6. The raw cross-frame depth error in Eq. 7 also lacks scale/shift alignment or normalization. Monocular depth and pose scale ambiguity can therefore confound scores across videos, models, resolutions, and domains.

The controlled perturbation study is not a clean end-to-end validation. Some corruptions directly alter tracks while holding RGB or depth fixed, and others jointly manipulate intermediate inputs. These deliberately constructed cross-modal conflicts almost guarantee increases in metrics computed from those same quantities, but do not show that the complete pipeline responds correctly when only a video is geometrically degraded and all estimators are rerun.

The final score is cohort-dependent: normalization bounds and PCA weights are learned on the full evaluation dataset, so adding new methods or outliers can change existing scores. PCA maximizes variance rather than agreement with geometric-consistency ground truth, its loading sign is arbitrary, and the paper retains two translation components with correlation about 0.992, effectively double-counting one signal. Cross-validating weight stability does not resolve the absence of an externally calibrated test set or validate the semantics of PC1.

Several conclusions overstate the evidence. Correlations of 0.44 and 0.52 between SGC and camera dynamics, and 0.79 for Latte, do not support the claim that the metric is inherently robust to camera motion. No confidence intervals or uncertainty tests are reported for model comparisons, despite unequal sample counts and differences in task, resolution, duration, and content. Distribution-level FVD against Kinetics is also not a direct baseline for per-video geometric consistency.

The advertised scope is broader than the implemented measure. SGC explicitly discards moving regions and thus primarily evaluates static-background consistency, yet the paper claims to diagnose object impermanence and catastrophic dynamic-object collapse. Its own mask study shows that under-segmentation can change scores by over 100% or spuriously improve them. Fixed 1D depth clustering can merge disconnected surfaces, while four-point PnP on narrow or coplanar regions may be poorly conditioned; solver failure rates and sensitivity to these choices are not reported. These unresolved issues prevent the current evidence from supporting SGC as a reliable benchmark, although the underlying diagnostic direction is promising.

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation gap: conventional video-quality metrics can miss 3D background distortions, while temporal-consistency metrics can be confounded by legitimate foreground motion.
The local-pose-consensus idea is physically motivated and yields interpretable components for local rigidity, global-pose agreement, and depth consistency.

The empirical study is reasonably broad, covering 1,296 real and generated videos, ten generators, several baselines, controlled perturbations, component ablations, and an informative analysis of motion-mask sensitivity.
The manuscript is generally clear, and the appendix provides algorithms, component weights, and major hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central construct is not validated against independent ground truth. There is no human perceptual study, annotated ranking of geometric failures, or dataset with ground-truth camera poses and geometry. Separating real from generated datasets and showing monotonicity under hand-designed corruptions does not establish that SGC ranks naturally occurring failures correctly or better than baselines.

The translation terms appear technically under-specified and potentially invalid. Local PnP translation is obtained using Video Depth Anything depth, whereas the global translation comes from VGGT. The paper does not describe aligning their coordinate gauges or scales. Directly computing Euclidean differences between these translations in Eq. 6 may therefore compare incompatible quantities. Absolute cross-frame depth error in Eq. 7 is likewise sensitive to depth scale and scene depth, with no stated scale alignment or normalization.

The controlled validation is partly circular. Some perturbations directly modify tracks or estimated depth—the quantities consumed by SGC—rather than perturbing only video pixels and rerunning the complete estimator pipeline. In particular, the perspective squeeze changes only tracks while leaving RGB fixed, creating an artificial cross-modal inconsistency. These tests demonstrate responsiveness to manipulated inputs but provide weak evidence about real generated-video failures.

Reliance on several learned estimators introduces substantial, insufficiently controlled confounding. The supplement shows that mask corruption can increase SGC by over 100% on RT-1 and can paradoxically improve scores on OpenVid and Cosmos. There is no comparable evaluation of depth, tracking, or VGGT failure and domain bias, nor any oracle-input study that separates metric behavior from estimator errors.

The claimed foreground isolation is inconsistent with the qualitative interpretation. The paper cites subject distortion, paddle morphing, and a car/person merger as successes of SGC, although such dynamic regions should be removed by the static-background mask. This leaves unclear whether the metric measures the explicitly claimed background geometry or benefits from mask leakage.

PCA maximizes variance, not agreement with geometric quality, so its loadings are not intrinsically valid or 'objective' quality weights. The weights and normalization are fitted on the evaluated benchmark, creating dataset dependence and possible leakage. Ten-fold stability on the same mixture does not demonstrate transfer to new generators or domains. The manuscript also inconsistently describes the calibration set as the full dataset versus 1,196 videos, and does not report the normalization statistics required to apply the metric reproducibly.

The experiments mainly report aggregate metric values without confidence intervals, significance tests, per-video ground-truth correlations, or retrieval/ranking accuracy. Consequently, statements that SGC is 'strictly more rigorous,' 'proves' isolation of geometry, or establishes real videos as a strict lower bound are not supported by the presented evidence.

Several implementation details remain ambiguous, including the definition of the mean rotation, handling of failed or underconstrained PnP estimates, temporal aggregation, resolution/frame sampling, PCA sign handling, and the claimed [0,1] normalization—the supplied algorithm clips only below zero, not above one. The blank code field further weakens the reproducibility case. strengths: The submission is best viewed as a Datasets/Benchmarks-style evaluation-metric contribution rather than a new video-generation algorithm. Under that framing, it addresses an important and timely gap: existing fidelity and temporal metrics often fail to isolate background 3D geometric instability in generated videos.

SGC has an intuitive physical motivation: independently estimated camera motions for different static scene regions should agree in a rigid, coherent world. Combining local pose disagreement, disagreement with a global pose, and cross-frame depth consistency provides interpretable diagnostic components rather than only an opaque learned score.

The evaluation is broad, covering 1,296 videos, ten generative models across T2V/I2V/V2V settings, and three real-video domains. Comparisons with MEt3R, FVD, VBench, TRAJAN, and FVMD demonstrate useful complementarity and identify failures that appearance-oriented metrics can miss.

Controlled perturbation experiments show monotonic responses to warping, perspective squeeze, and depth deformation. The component-specific perturbations, architectural ablations, camera-motion analysis, and motion-mask sensitivity study collectively provide substantially more evidence than a simple model-ranking table.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with helpful pipeline diagrams, qualitative examples, pseudocode, component weights, hyperparameters, and dataset statistics. These details improve reproducibility and make the intended interpretation of the score relatively transparent.
weaknesses: The most important missing validation is agreement with human judgments or independently annotated geometric failures. Separation between real and generated datasets and sensitivity to hand-designed corruptions do not establish that SGC ranks naturally occurring generated-video failures according to perceptual severity. A blinded human study with pairwise rankings and failure-type annotations would considerably strengthen the central metric claim.

The metric is calibrated on the same full dataset used for the reported benchmark: PCA weights, Z-score statistics, and min-max bounds are learned from all evaluated videos. The ten-fold analysis tests stability of PCA weights, but does not clearly provide a fully held-out evaluation in which every normalization and weighting parameter is learned only from training folds. Consequently, scores are transductive, dataset-composition dependent, and potentially unstable for future models or out-of-distribution videos.

There is a significant technical ambiguity concerning scale. Local PnP translations are reconstructed using Video Depth Anything, whereas global translations come from VGGT; monocular depth and pose translations generally have arbitrary and potentially different scales. Equations comparing these translations directly, as well as the absolute depth-warping error, require an explicit scale-alignment or scale-invariant formulation that is not described. This could make several heavily weighted components sensitive to estimator scale rather than geometric consistency.

The controlled corruptions partly modify intermediate tracks or depth while holding other modalities fixed, rather than always corrupting an RGB video and rerunning the complete pipeline. Such tests verify that the score reacts to deliberately induced cross-modal disagreement, but provide weaker evidence about end-to-end behavior under realistic generation artifacts. Evaluation on rendered scenes with known geometry and camera trajectories would offer cleaner ground truth.

SGC depends on several large learned estimators and especially on motion segmentation. The supplement usefully demonstrates that under-segmentation can change scores by over 100% and can even spuriously improve them, but the paper does not provide estimator-failure rates, uncertainty estimates, handling of too few valid regions/tracks, or computational cost. This limits robustness and reproducibility in difficult generated clips.

The scope is narrower than some presentation suggests: the method deliberately measures static-background consistency and can mask out dynamic objects, yet the paper sometimes describes general video-level 3D consistency and illustrates failures involving moving subjects or objects. The claims should more consistently characterize SGC as a complementary background-geometry diagnostic, not a comprehensive measure of object permanence or dynamic-scene geometry.

Model comparisons are mostly reported as means without confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or uncertainty from stochastic segmentation/tracking/PnP. Moreover, the appendix alternates between 1,196 and 1,296 videos as the calibration-set size, and the stated normalization maps calibration data to [0,1] while Algorithm 2 clips only the lower bound, consistent with plotted scores exceeding 1. These issues should be clarified before the score is treated as standardized.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation gap: measuring static-scene 3D consistency in generated videos without penalizing legitimate foreground motion. The physically motivated comparison of camera poses estimated from different background regions is intuitive and potentially useful.

The evaluation is broad, covering 1,296 real and generated videos, ten generators, several baseline families, controlled perturbations, component ablations, motion-segmentation sensitivity, and alternative geometric estimators.

The estimator-replacement experiment shows encouraging ranking stability (Spearman rho at least 0.860), while the reported human study suggests stronger alignment with judgments of background stability than MEt3R and VBench.
The paper is generally clear, includes useful qualitative failure cases, and appropriately states that SGC evaluates static backgrounds rather than non-rigid foreground geometry.
weaknesses: The score contains potentially incompatible and unnormalized geometric quantities. Local PnP translation inherits the scale of Video Depth Anything, whereas global translation comes from VGGT, but no scale alignment between these systems is specified before their direct comparison in Eq. 6. Likewise, Eq. 7 uses absolute depth differences without normalization for scene scale or depth-estimator scale. These issues undermine cross-video and cross-domain comparability.

The controlled experiments are not convincingly end-to-end. Some perturbations directly modify tracks or depth while leaving RGB unchanged, or jointly alter cached intermediate representations. Such constructed cross-modal conflicts are almost guaranteed to increase a metric built from those representations; the stronger test would perturb/render the input videos and rerun every estimator.

The aggregation is dataset-dependent and partly transductive: PCA weights, z-score statistics, and min-max bounds are learned using the full evaluation dataset. Cross-validation only establishes weight stability, not generalization of complete scores to unseen models or domains. The normalization statistics and bounds needed to reproduce SGC are not reported, and Algorithm 2 lower-clips but does not upper-clip despite claiming a [0,1] score.

Human validation is encouraging but statistically weak: 1,050 pairwise decisions are collapsed to only 11 entity-level observations, with no confidence intervals, inter-annotator agreement, pair-sampling distribution, or significance test for improvements over baselines. This does not robustly establish the claimed perceptual superiority.

Motion masking can censor precisely the generated warping or morphing that the metric seeks to detect, because such artifacts may be labeled dynamic and removed. The sensitivity study itself reports that mask errors can reduce SGC substantially, yet no rejection criterion or uncertainty estimate is supplied for unreliable masks.

Several important implementation cases remain undefined, including the rotation-mean computation, handling of failed or poorly conditioned PnP estimates, insufficient valid regions, depth-scale alignment, and inference normalization for out-of-distribution videos. The blank code link compounds the reproducibility concern for a metric paper.

Overall, this is a promising Algorithms/General contribution with substantial empirical work, but the scale/gauge ambiguity, dataset-calibrated score, and non-end-to-end validation leave the central claim of a transferable quantitative 3D-consistency metric insufficiently established.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored evaluation problem: generated videos can look plausible frame by frame while violating static-scene geometry. Measuring this separately from foreground dynamics would be valuable to the video-generation community.

The central intuition is physically motivated and interpretable: static regions should induce compatible camera transformations, so disagreement among region-wise PnP estimates can reveal non-rigid background behavior.

The evaluation is relatively broad, covering 1,296 videos, ten generators, three real-video sources, several baseline metrics, synthetic perturbations, component ablations, alternative geometry estimators, and a human study.

The manuscript includes useful robustness analyses, particularly camera-motion stratification, motion-mask corruption, and estimator replacement. It also candidly identifies dependence on pretrained estimators and exclusion of non-rigid foreground geometry as limitations.
The presentation is generally organized and understandable, with helpful pipeline and qualitative illustrations.
weaknesses: There is a fundamental unresolved scale/coordinate-system issue. Local PnP translations are recovered from Video Depth Anything depths, whereas global translations come from VGGT. The paper does not explain how the two independently estimated coordinate systems and scales are aligned before computing the global translation discrepancy in Eq. 6. Monocular depth scale can also vary across videos. This directly threatens two heavily weighted score components and hence cross-video rankings.

The depth-consistency term in Eq. 7 is an absolute depth difference, without an explained scale alignment, normalization by scene depth, or treatment of monocular-depth gauge ambiguity. Consequently, it may reflect scene scale, estimator calibration, or dataset characteristics rather than geometric consistency. This is especially concerning because depth error receives a large PCA weight.

The final score is dataset-relative and partly calibrated on the evaluation set itself: z-score statistics, min/max bounds, and PCA weights are learned from the full 1,296-video collection used for the reported comparison. Cross-validation only demonstrates stability within that collection; it does not show that a frozen metric transfers to unseen generators or domains. The paper also does not clearly specify how future videos outside the calibration range should be handled, and Algorithm 2 clips only the lower bound despite describing a [0,1] score.

PCA maximizes variance, not validity or agreement with geometric inconsistency. Thus calling its weights objective does not establish that they form a meaningful quality score. In particular, the two translation components have correlation approximately 0.992 and jointly receive nearly half the total weight; describing this redundancy as intentional does not demonstrate that the resulting double counting is desirable.

The synthetic tests are substantially circular. Some corrupt estimated tracks while leaving RGB unchanged, or jointly manipulate RGB, tracks, and depth instead of rerunning the complete estimators on a corrupted video. These interventions directly alter the quantities appearing in the proposed equations and therefore mainly confirm algebraic sensitivity, not end-to-end validity under realistic generation failures.

The human validation is too weakly reported to support the headline correlation. Although there are 1,050 pairwise judgments, correlations are computed after aggregation to only 11 entities. No confidence intervals, significance comparisons between metrics, inter-annotator agreement, pair-sampling details, or instance-level analysis are given. Aggregating all real datasets into one entity further obscures variability and can inflate apparent rank agreement.

The benchmark confounds model quality with source-dataset properties. Models differ in task, resolution, duration, content, and likely camera-motion distributions, and the manuscript does not establish prompt- or content-matched comparisons. Treating real datasets as geometric ground truth is also unjustified because they can contain rolling shutter, depth-estimation failures, and imperfect motion segmentation.

Several operational details necessary for reproducibility and robustness are missing: handling of failed or ill-conditioned PnP estimates, frames with fewer than two valid regions, confidence-weighted aggregation, depth invalidity and occlusions, the exact rotation-mean computation, estimator preprocessing, runtime, and failure rates. The displayed code field is blank.

The metric can hide precisely the failures it aims to detect: warped or morphing background regions may be labeled as moving by SegAnyMo and removed. The mask-corruption study even observes that omitting difficult regions can spuriously improve SGC, but no coverage statistic, abstention mechanism, or safeguard against such metric gaming is provided.

Overall, the idea has promise, but the unresolved geometric-scale validity, evaluation-set calibration, and insufficient independent validation are consequential rather than cosmetic. They prevent the current results from establishing SGC as a reliable, model-agnostic metric.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-served evaluation problem: measuring static-background 3D consistency without penalizing valid foreground motion. The physical intuition—static regions should imply a common camera transformation—is clear and compelling.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 1,296 videos, ten generative models, three real-video domains, several baselines, controlled corruptions, component ablations, alternative geometry estimators, and motion-segmentation sensitivity.

The metric has encouraging empirical support. SGC responds monotonically to the tested perturbations, generally separates real from generated videos, preserves rankings across alternative geometry backbones (Spearman rho at least 0.860), and correlates strongly with the targeted human judgments (rho 0.945).

The manuscript is well organized and visually clear. It provides component definitions, algorithms, hyperparameters, PCA weights, limitations, and useful qualitative diagnoses of different geometric failure modes.
weaknesses: A core technical ambiguity undermines the score definition. Local PnP translations are reconstructed using Video Depth Anything, whereas global translations come from VGGT. These systems generally have independent or arbitrary scales, but the paper specifies no scale alignment before directly comparing translations in Eq. 6 or warping depths in Eq. 7. Because global/local translation and depth terms receive most of the PCA weight, this is consequential rather than a minor implementation omission.

SGC is not demonstrated to be an intrinsic, portable metric. Z-score statistics, min/max bounds, and PCA weights are learned on the full evaluation dataset, including the videos being ranked. Cross-validation only examines weight stability and does not address leakage through normalization or behavior on a genuinely held-out dataset. Algorithm 2 also applies only a lower-bound clip, contradicting the claimed [0,1] normalization.

The controlled perturbations do not consistently validate the end-to-end metric on visibly corrupted videos. Some tests alter tracks while leaving RGB unchanged, or jointly modify RGB and supplied tracks while holding estimated depth fixed. These cross-modal interventions bypass the behavior of the actual depth and tracking estimators and may manufacture precisely the inconsistencies that SGC is designed to detect.

The human evaluation is reduced to correlations over only 11 aggregated entities, despite collecting 1,050 pairwise judgments. No confidence intervals, inter-annotator agreement, statistical comparison between metrics, or clip-level correlation is reported. Entity-level aggregation can make the reported rho appear substantially stronger than sample-level generalization warrants.

Several robustness concerns remain insufficiently controlled: score dependence on scene depth scale and content, PnP degeneracy or failure coverage, uncertainty from using as few as four correspondences, and mask leakage. Camera dynamics correlate substantially with SGC for some real datasets and very strongly for Latte (r=0.79), which weakens the claim that the metric is inherently motion-independent.

Model-level comparisons confound geometric quality with task, resolution, duration, content distribution, and conditioning paradigm; for example, the strongest generated result is a V2V model while most others are T2V or I2V. Confidence intervals or matched-content comparisons are needed before interpreting the resulting ordering as a reliable ranking of generators.

Overall, the idea and empirical effort are promising, but the unaddressed coordinate-scale issue and dataset-dependent calibration prevent the current manuscript from establishing a technically well-defined, reusable metric. This places it slightly below the acceptance threshold despite its potential impact.
